episode.subject: juvenile hawksbill turtle with remoras
episode.title: I said I was going back
episode.body:
I was quite small when a fish settled on my shell. I asked where he wanted to go. He said wherever I was going.

I tried to make that somewhere good. Took a long curve over the sand instead of turning back. Another fish joined us. Then another.

By the time I wanted to turn, I was afraid everyone would notice I hadn't known where I was going.

I said I was going back.

Nobody left.

proposals.visibleScene: A juvenile hawksbill above pale sandy bottom, flippers extended, several slender remoras aligned along its carapace and small attached barnacles. Turtle and passengers are legible; moderate underwater green cast.
proposals.fictionBoundary: Joining order, conversation, route, wish to impress, turn and continued attachment are authored fiction. Observer documents a27cm juvenile foraging with remoras and barnacles, not these actions. No photograph establishes sex.
proposals.continuity: Insert before every existing Rhea episode as explicitly juvenile memory. Preserve adult female casting, Little Cayman home and avatar. Photograph is from Rose Atoll in the Pacific, not Little Cayman. It illustrates the same globally distributed species; do not assert that canon Rhea traveled between those populations. Existing held A passenger with opinions and current-chosen-route passages remain unchanged. This is an early mistake about what companions expect, not another banking attempt to dislodge a rider.
proposals.authorReview: The passengers are visibly present. Rhea invents a duty to provide a destination, then risks admitting she wants to return. Their staying resolves that specific fear. Distinct from her admitted school adjusting to her speed. Geography is an explicit illustration limitation for lead judgment.

episode.subject: blue-legged hermit crab in a held shell
episode.title: The shell is occupied
episode.body:
I had pulled all my legs in when the shell began to rise.

I waited inside for it to stop. It stopped, but the ground did not come back.

I came out very slowly.

The soft thing holding my home is enormous. I have put out one leg.

I would like it to know the shell is occupied.

proposals.visibleScene: Human fingers hold a green striped gastropod shell. Blue-legged hermit crab projects blue banded legs from aperture. Black background, strong shell/leg detail, softer dark face. No leg visibly grips or touches a finger.
proposals.fictionBoundary: Withdrawal, lifting sequence, waiting, emergence, intention and inability to reach ground are invented around the actual held shell. No claim that the source observer harmed, rescued or returned the crab. No invented grip, injury or eye contact. Second photo shows a more withdrawn state but does not document the narrated order.
proposals.continuity: Existing Clibanarius tricolor identity, Key Largo home, bio and avatar unchanged. Monroe County source compatible with home region. Insert before current held shell-search drafts; no growth, molt, reproductive event or new shell acquisition. Drafts stay preserved.
proposals.authorReview: Fear produces a small act of self-disclosure to the holder, not a triumphant escape or rescue. It is a complete change of response with an unresolved external situation. Image caveat is material: blue legs are much clearer than the face, and human fingers occupy significant frame space. Root should hold if its exact rendering fails the visual bar.

media.description:
27cm SCL juvenile hawksbill turtle foraging in the lagoon at Rose Atoll just off Rose Island. Embedding gooseneck barnacles and Remora sp are a bonus! 

This observation was included as part of the below study on the spatial population structure, and specifically the developmental biogeography, for the species. Serving the broader interest of open-access science, and as senior author on this study, I am archiving these images here, using iNaturalist as a third-party repository.

https://doi.org/10.1002/ece3.2034
https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ece3.2034
